content.title: Detecting and Mitigating Indirect Stereotypes in Word Embeddings
content.abstract: Societal biases in the usage of words, including harmful stereotypes, are frequently learned by common word embedding methods.  These biases manifest not only between a word and an explicit marker of its stereotype, but also between words that share related stereotypes.  This latter phenomenon, sometimes called ``indirect bias,'' has resisted prior attempts at debiasing.  In this paper, we propose a novel method to mitigate indirect bias in distributional word embeddings by modifying biased relationships between words before embeddings are learned.  This is done by considering how the co-occurrence probability of a given pair of words changes in the presence of words marking an attribute of bias, and using this to average out the effect of a bias attribute.  To evaluate this method, we perform a series of common tests and demonstrate that the semantic quality of the word embeddings is retained while measures of bias in the embeddings are reduced.  In addition, we conduct novel tests for measuring indirect stereotypes by extending the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) with new test sets for indirect binary gender stereotypes.  With these tests, we demonstrate that this method can reduce the presence of more subtle stereotypes not properly addressed by previous work.
